para: Two components carry the signal. Removing the rule-engine vote from fusion cost 12.1 points of flat recall@5 (-14.4 to -9.8) and removing the expert syndrome layer alone cost 9.5 points (-11.1 to -7.9). The remaining layers contributed little on this task: the Bayesian network -1.3 points, the fuzzy and knowledge-graph layers and the risk models each within ±0.5 points (the risk-model layer changed no ranking at all), and the fusion refinements—Yager versus Dempster combination, discord shrinkage, single-source discount—within ±0.5 points; collapsing the fusion weights to uniform cost 1.4 points. Most importantly for the reviewer's question about the AI-drafted registry: restricting the registry to the 272 manually curated anchor rules and switching off the 32,911 AI-assisted rules changed flat recall@5 by only -0.9 points (-2.1 to +0.2), two-tier recall@5 by -3.0 points and mean per-group AUROC from 0.767 to 0.732. On clinician-listed ICU diagnoses, therefore, the large AI-drafted rule base adds breadth and discrimination at the margin but is not what drives the headline recall; the hand-curated anchors and the syndrome layer are. Removing the 28 `unverified_source` rules changed recall@5 by +0.0 points. We regard this as reassuring for safety (the unaudited rules are not load-bearing) and as a limit on the claim that scale of the registry is itself an advantage; its value, if any, lies in coverage of rarer entities that the eICU label set does not test.
